title: Plan the firewall change
scenario: Copperleaf Garden Centers has a head office and nine stores. The card terminals in every store reach the payment system through a single firewall at head office. Copperleaf is moving its home deliveries to a new courier, Brisk Parcel, whose servers will send delivery updates to Copperleaf's order server. This needs a firewall change: a new network segment for the order server, and an allow rule that admits Brisk Parcel's two addresses on HTTPS only. Applying the change restarts the firewall, which cuts the stores off for about five minutes. Marta Lindqvist, the e-commerce manager, needs the change and has proposed Sunday from 02:00 to 04:00, when every store is closed. Two network engineers will do the work. You are the engineer who plans the change.

steps.prompt: Copperleaf's change procedure has three rules. No work is done on a change until its request has been logged. The lab test is planned from the impact analysis. The change advisory board decides only when it has both the impact analysis and the test results. Put the steps of the firewall change in order, from first to last.

items.text: The change advisory board reviews the request, the impact analysis and the test results, and approves the change and its window
The engineers check that the card terminals reach the payment system and that Brisk Parcel's updates arrive, and restore the saved configuration if a check fails
Marta submits a change request that describes the new segment and rule, the reason for them and the proposed Sunday window
The network records are brought up to date and the change record is closed
The engineers apply the change to a spare firewall in the lab, run their checks and record the results
The store managers and the help desk are sent the date and time of the approved window
The engineers work out what the change touches and what could go wrong, including the stores' card terminals and the five-minute restart
At 02:00 on Sunday the engineers save the running configuration, then add the new segment and rule

steps.explanation: The path of a change is request, impact analysis, test, approval, maintenance window, implementation, verification or backout, and updated documentation. Copperleaf's rules fix the early steps: the request comes first, the test is planned from the impact analysis, and the board will not decide without the test results, so testing comes before approval. The window is proposed in the request and approved with it, so the stakeholders can be told the approved time only after the board has decided, and they must hear it before the work starts. The work then waits for the window, the result is verified with the backout ready, and the change is finished only when the records match the system.

steps.prompt: Match each responsibility in this change to the person or group that holds it.

left.text: Deciding whether the change may go ahead, after reading the impact analysis and the test results
Carrying out the approved work during the window, and nothing beyond it
Answering for the change from request to sign-off, and confirming that delivery updates arrive as the business needs
Sitting on the board to ask whether the new rule opens more than Brisk Parcel needs
Being consulted about the effect on the stores and told when the work will happen

right.text: The store managers and the help desk

steps.explanation: Marta needs the change and is accountable for it, which makes her the owner. Owning a change is not the same as doing the work or approving it. The store managers and the help desk are stakeholders: the change affects them, so they are consulted and informed. The change advisory board is the approval body and makes the decision, using the impact analysis and the test results as evidence. The security manager is the board member who asks whether the change opens anything up. The network engineers implement the change, and the approval covers that work and nothing more. Owner: accountable. Stakeholders: affected. Board: decides. Engineers: carry it out.

steps.prompt: The impact analysis lists six ways in which the change could go wrong. Sort each one by the security goal it would harm.

items.text: The allow rule is written for any source address, and a stranger on the internet downloads customers' delivery addresses from the order server
The firewall does not come back after its restart, and no store's card terminals can reach the payment system
The order server is given write access to the stock database by mistake, and an intruder on the order server alters the recorded prices
A mistyped address in the rule shuts out Brisk Parcel's servers, and no delivery updates can be received
The rule also admits unencrypted HTTP, and someone on the path alters a delivery update from "failed" to "delivered" in transit
The new segment is given a route to the HR server by mistake, and an intruder on the order server reads staff salary records

steps.explanation: Ask what was actually harmed. When systems or data cannot be reached by those who need them, as with the firewall that stays down and the courier that is shut out, availability is harmed. When information is read by someone who should not see it, as with the delivery addresses and the salary records, confidentiality is harmed. When information is changed without permission, as with the altered delivery update and the altered prices, integrity is harmed. A security-minded impact analysis looks for all three, not only for an outage.

steps.prompt: The backout plan needs a decision point. The window runs from 02:00 to 04:00 on Sunday. If the change fails, restoring the saved configuration, restarting the firewall and repeating the checks takes about 30 minutes. Which line should the backout plan contain?

options.text: If any check is still failing at 04:00, ask the board for a longer window.
If any check is still failing at 03:45, restore the saved configuration.
If the change seems to be going badly, the engineers agree what to do next.
If any check is still failing at 03:15, restore the saved configuration.

why.a: By 04:00 the window has closed with the firewall still failing its checks. The backout must be finished inside the approved window, and work after 04:00 is outside what was approved.
why.b: This leaves 15 minutes for a backout that takes about 30, so the firewall would still be in an uncertain state when the window closes at 04:00.
why.c: A decision point is a clear condition and a time, agreed in advance. Leaving it to judgment on the night invites the team to keep trying until it is too late to go back.
why.d: Correct. It names a condition and a time, and it leaves 45 minutes for a 30-minute backout, so the old configuration is running again before the window closes.

steps.explanation: A backout plan needs something to go back to, written restore steps and a decision point. The decision point must come early enough for the backout to finish before the maintenance window closes.

steps.prompt: At 02:40 every check passes, so no backout is needed. Which three records must be brought up to date before the change is closed? (Choose three.)

options.text: The test results, which show the figures from the lab firewall and not those from the live one
The network diagram, which does not show the order server's new segment
The acceptable use policy for staff, which does not mention Brisk Parcel's connection
The help desk's procedure for missing delivery updates, which covers only the old courier's connection
The impact analysis, which lists several risks that did not happen on the night
The firewall configuration in version control, which is still the pre-change version

why.a: Test results are evidence of what happened in the lab before approval. They stay in the change record as they were, and the outcome of the live change is recorded separately.
why.b: Correct. The change added a network segment, so the diagram no longer matches the network. An out-of-date diagram misleads whoever next has to trace a fault or an attack.
why.c: The acceptable use policy sets rules for how staff use Copperleaf's systems. A courier's server connection does not change those rules.
why.d: Correct. The change alters how delivery updates reach Copperleaf, so the written procedure for that fault must change with it.
why.e: The impact analysis is part of the audit trail that shows what the approvers knew when they decided. It is kept, not edited afterward.
why.f: Correct. The repository must hold the newly approved configuration. Otherwise a later comparison with the live firewall would flag the approved change as unauthorized, and a later backout would return to the wrong version.

steps.explanation: A change is finished when the records match the system. Update the diagrams, the procedures that the change affects and the version-controlled configuration. Keep the change record itself, with its impact analysis, test results and outcome, as the audit trail.
